content:
New Zealand Winegrowers (NZW) has released its 2026 Annual Report, with exports reaching $2.108 billion and export volume increasing to 306.2 million litres in the 12 months to June 2026.

NZW said the result “reflects an overall sales increase of 8% driven by export growth and represents the industry’s second-highest June year total on record”.

“In the face of a challenging global and domestic environment, New Zealand wine continued to outperform the wider category in key markets, providing grounds for confidence in the long-term prospects of New Zealand wine,” it said.

Meanwhile, individual businesses across the sector were making adjustments. Vintage 2026 delivered a smaller harvest of approximately 440,000 tonnes, down a significant 15% on the previous year, bringing production “into closer balance with current market demand and supporting the industry’s focus on sustainable long-term growth”.

Fabian Yukich, chair of New Zealand Winegrowers, said the report showed an industry that was far from standing still.

“This has been a challenging year across the global wine industry, but New Zealand wine continues to show remarkable resilience.

“What stands out is the determination of growers and wineries to adapt. Businesses in the sector are making adjustments, the progress made this year gives us confidence that it is moving towards a more balanced footing”.

Yukich added that the report demonstrated the sector’s resilience.

“Consumers around the world continue to discover, love and buy New Zealand wines. Our focus is on supporting members through the immediate challenges while continuing to strengthen the opportunities that will carry the industry forward.”

CEO Anishka Jelicich, who was appointed to the role in July, said the Annual Report marked the start of the next phase for NZW, guided by its new strategy.

“Our new strategy has a clear purpose: to elevate and sustain the New Zealand wine industry by empowering our members,” Jelicich said.

“This means giving growers and wineries the information, advocacy and practical support they need to make well-informed decisions.”

Jelicich said NZW’s focus would be on turning the strategy into value for members.

“Our role is to support the industry as a whole so that New Zealand wine can emerge stronger and succeed over the long term”.

content:
Robyn Puglisi-Henderson is now the fourth member of the Puglisi family to receive the award. Images supplied

Robyn Puglisi-Henderson, business manager at Ballandean Estate Wines, has been honoured with the 2026 Samuel Bassett Award at the 42nd Annual Queensland Wine Awards.

The award is the Queensland wine industry’s highest mark of tribute, recognising long-term contribution and leadership.

Puglisi-Henderson is a fourth-generation member of the Puglisi family, the founders and custodians of Queensland’s oldest family-run winery, Ballandean Estate.

She has played a “vital role in the growth and resilience of the business for more than 25 years, since returning to the estate in 1999”.

“Among Robyn’s standout achievements is developing the estate’s export trade from zero to 20 per cent of business turnover in just five years, including establishing a market in China for the Granite Belt’s premium red wine,” said Adam Penberthy, president of the Queensland Wine Industry Association.

“The Samuel Bassett Award celebrates those who believe in what we do, who aren’t afraid to hold our ground in the face of the doubters, and who leave the industry better placed than they found it.”

Robyn with Adam Penberthy, president of the Queensland Wine Industry Association.

With this win, Robyn becomes the fourth member of the Puglisi family to receive the Samuel Bassett Award, following her father Angelo Puglisi (2003), her mother Mary Puglisi (2015) and her sister Leeanne Puglisi-Gangemi (2019).

“We opened the cellar the year I was born. I think I’ve spent more time there talking to people than I have at home! Being part of the Granite Belt’s tourism story for over 50 years is an honour. This week, we saw Stanthorpe awarded Gold at the 2026 Australian Top Tourism Town Awards. What a journey,” exclaimed Robyn Puglisi-Henderson.

“I was raised in a proud winemaking family. and it is my job and my hobby to champion Queensland wine. It is a pleasure to be part of such a great community who share the same passion for premium wine and visitor experiences.”

The winery shared that her work reflects the “essential, often less visible efforts that sustain a regional wine industry: building resilient businesses, creating new markets, supporting people and ensuring that the achievements of one generation become the foundations for the next”. Her contribution to the wider community was also recognised in 2016, when she received a Paul Harris Fellow Award for Community Service.

The Samuel Bassett Award is named for wine industry pioneer Samuel Symons Bassett, who hauled the first wine grape cuttings to Roma in 1863, laying an early foundation for winemaking in Queensland.

content:
Ian McKendrick, the newly appointed executive director of APISWA. Image supplied

The Asia Pacific International Spirits and Wines Alliance (APISWA) has appointed Ian McKendrick as its new executive director.

McKendrick will lead the Alliance’s engagement with governments, regulators and industry stakeholders across Asia Pacific, working with its 10 member companies to “strengthen the sector’s voice, promote evidence-based policy and support responsible growth”.

“I am delighted to be joining APISWA. Asia Pacific is one of the most dynamic and significant regions for the international spirits and wine industry, and the policy environment is evolving rapidly across its markets.

“I look forward to working with our members, governments and partners to help shape that environment, from trade and taxation to responsible consumption and the fight against illicit alcohol, in ways that benefit consumers, local communities, and the wider economies in which our members operate,” McKendrick said.

Ludovic Ledru, chairman of APISWA, said the organisation is pleased to welcome McKendrick.

“His experience at the Scotch Whisky Association and in international trade diplomacy, including in China, makes him well suited to lead the Alliance at a time when the regulatory and policy landscape across Asia Pacific is becoming increasingly complex.

“Ian’s understanding of how governments, industry, and stakeholders can work together will be a real asset as we continue to champion the interests of our members and the responsible enjoyment of spirits and wine across the region,” Ledru said.

He joins APISWA from the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO). Prior to that, he spent six years at the Scotch Whisky Association (SWA), where he was international director, leading the association’s work to support the global growth of Scotch Whisky across more than 160 markets. He also spent more than two decades in the FCO, including postings at the British Embassy in Beijing and four years in the Directorate-General for Trade at the European Commission as a seconded national expert on China. His broader diplomatic career spanned economic and trade issues, including as lead negotiator for post-Brexit international agreements in the Middle East and North Africa.

Clare Valley winery Kilikanoon Wines has taken home the title of ‘Best Producer Australia’ as well as the award for ‘Best Australian Red of Show’ with its Attunga 1865 Shiraz 2022 at the 2026 Mundus Vini Grand International Wine Awards.

The Mundus Vini awards are judged internationally, with wines assessed alongside entries from leading producers around the world.

Kilikanoon said the result is particularly meaningful given its long history of success at Mundus Vini, having previously been named ‘Best Australian Producer’ a record nine times.

Kilikanoon CEO Travis Fuller said the result was a great reflection of the team and the wines being made at the winery.

“To be named ‘Best Australian Producer’ and then have Attunga 1865 named ‘Best Australian Red of Show’, is a pretty special result for the team.

“There are some incredible Australian producers putting wines into these competitions, so to come out on top is something we’re really proud of.

“And to have that recognition come alongside another ‘Top 5 Red Star’ result from Halliday is a great reflection of the consistency of the wines we’re making.”

At the centre of the Mundus Vini result is the Attunga 1865 Shiraz, made from fruit grown on Kilikanoon’s historic Attunga vineyard. Planted in 1865, the vineyard is one of the Clare Valley’s oldest continuously producing Shiraz vineyards and has long been an important part of Kilikanoon’s premium red wine collection.

“It’s a great result for Clare Valley as well,” said Fuller.

“We know how good the wines being made here are, so it’s pretty special to see one of our wines recognised at this level.”

Kilikanoon Wines was established in 1997 and is based at a restored 1860s farmhouse in Penwortham, Clare Valley.

Coonawarra is set to come alive this October with three weekends of Cabernet Celebrations. Image supplied

The Coonawarra Cabernet Celebrations are set to return this year from 1-18 October across three weekends of wine, food, music and regional experiences.

Celebrating Coonawarra’s signature variety, Cabernet Sauvignon, this year’s festival features more than 40 free and ticketed experiences across the region, “inviting visitors to meet the makers, explore the vineyards and cellar doors and discover just why Coonawarra Cabernet has earned an international reputation”.

Coonawarra Vignerons acting executive officer Heidi Guyett said the program of events provides a perfect reason to visit the region in spring.

“October is a fantastic time to experience Coonawarra. The vineyards are bursting back to life, the days are getting longer and there’s a wonderful energy throughout the region.

“Aside from tasting the exquisite wines of the region, visitors will have the opportunity to meet and dine with winemakers, viticulturists and boutique winery owners, go behind the scenes in the winery and even sample wines that are yet to be officially released, all the while learning about the process and the passion that goes into Coonawarra’s famed wines,” Guyett shared.

‘Something different every weekend’

The celebrations will begin over the October SA Labour Day long weekend, with the popular ‘Coonawarra Cabernet Celebrations Golf Day’ teeing off at Penola Golf Course on Friday 2 October.

The all-inclusive Ambrose event combines golf with sparkling Cabernet, regional food and Coonawarra wine, with teams competing for the “coveted Champion Team red jackets”.

Across the long weekend, visitors can also roll up their sleeves for ‘Pasta Making & Lunch with the DiGiorgio Family’, take a guided vineyard tour at Rymill Coonawarra, enjoy sparkling Cabernet at Sunset at Balnaves, or settle in for live music, pizza and family-friendly festivities at wineries across the region.

New to the festival in 2026, the ‘Coonawarra Community Markets’ will make their Cabernet Celebrations debut on Sunday 4 October, “showcasing the best of local with fresh produce, handmade and handcrafted goods, artisan wares and Coonawarra wines, all coming together in a vibrant community market atmosphere”.

The weekend of the 9 -11 October invites visitors to ‘Blend It Up’, with Cabernet Gin in the spotlight at Parker Estate, ‘Cocktails on the Deck’ on offer at Brand’s Laira and a relaxed afternoon of pizza and live music at Zema Estate.

The festival culminates with a feature-packed final weekend, led by the ‘Cabernet Decade[nce] Tasting and Dinner’ on Friday 16 October. Up to 15 Coonawarra producers will come together at Wynns Coonawarra Estate for a one-night-only tasting showcasing Cabernet Sauvignon with age, followed by an optional degustation dinner at the Ottelia Restaurant.

Saturday 17 October with feature Yalumba’s barrel Cooper demonstration at the Menzies Coonawarra property, set to be a highlight among the traditional offerings, including Bowen Estate’s ‘En Primeur’, a special ‘Decade of Majella Cabernet’ vertical tasting and ‘Prof’s Paella’ at Majella.

Another new addition to the program is the highly anticipated ‘Band on the Bus – Tipples and Tunes Road Tour’, combining great wine and live music in one roving day out. Guests will hop aboard for a tour of three wineries with Lady & The Amp jumping off the bus to perform a live set at each stop along the way.

Haylie Gregor from Lady & The Amp said the pair were looking forward to taking their music on the road.

“We’re really excited to bring the Band on the Bus concept into the Cabernet Celebrations program for the first time. It’s going to be a great day of Coonawarra wine, live music and plenty of laughs, and we can’t wait to have everyone on board.”

The program also features unique dining experiences such as ‘Brand’s Laira’s Dinner’ in Erics historic Cellar and Raidis Estate’s ‘Murder in the Vines – Mystery Dinner’ where guests are invited to “step back in time for an immersive evening of costumes, mystery and Coonawarra history, inspired by colourful characters from the region’s past”.

“Last year’s ‘Murder in the Vines’ was an absolute hit, so we knew we had to bring it back for another instalment,” said Raidis Estate co-owner Emma Raidis.

“It’s everything we love at Raidis — great wine, good food, plenty of laughs and people coming together.

“Guests are encouraged to embrace the 1920s theme, dress the part and immerse themselves in the story. If last year is anything to go by, there’ll be plenty of accusations, surprises and laughs along the way.”

‘Cabernet beyond the current vintage’

For those wanting to delve deeper, Cabernet Celebrations “provides a rare opportunity to discover Coonawarra wines across vintages, producers and styles”.

Museum wines, vertical tastings, pre-release wines and specially curated flights will feature throughout October, alongside experiences exploring food and wine pairings, vineyard stories and the “remarkable ageing potential” of Coonawarra Cabernet Sauvignon.

“One of the great things about the festival is the access it gives visitors to wines and experiences they might not ordinarily encounter,” Guyett said.

“There are opportunities to taste Cabernet across decades, try wines before release, walk through the vineyards and hear directly from the people who grow and make them. But equally, you can come along for pizza, music and a glass of wine on the lawn. There really is something for every kind of visitor.”

‘Leave the car behind’

For those venturing to the region, Coonawarra Vignerons emphasised that navigating the region “is a breeze with the region’s cellar doors all scattered along one stretch of road”.

Making it easier to explore the region, the ‘Coonawarra Cabernet Celebrations Hop On-Hop Off Shuttle Bus’ will operate exclusively on Saturdays 3, 10 and 17 October.

Nearby Blue Lake City residents can also ditch their keys with a newly introduced service from Mount Gambier departing at 10am, “making a day trip to Coonawarra easier than ever”.

Local hop-on hop-off tickets from Penola/Coonawarra are $23.50 per person, while the Mount Gambier return service, including all-day hop-on hop-off access, is $40 per person.

The shuttle is about making it easy for people to enjoy a full day in Coonawarra,” Guyett said.

“Whether you’re staying locally or visiting from Mount Gambier, you can leave the car behind, hop between participating wineries and events, and simply enjoy the day.”

Visitors are encouraged to book early, particularly for ticketed events, accommodation and Saturday shuttle services.

Treasury Wine Estates (TWE) has announced it will sell Seppelt to Aaron Drummond, CEO and co-owner of respected Mornington Peninsula winery Stonier, and partners.

The sale includes the Seppelt brand, the Great Western winery, cellar door and vineyards, and the Drumborg vineyard near Portland.

At its June Investor Day, TWE announced plans to explore the sale of “non-core brands and assets” as part of its “broader transformation to create a more focused brand portfolio and simplified production footprint”.

Treasury Wine Estates managing director, Australia & New Zealand and Europe, Angus Lilley said the sale was a positive outcome for Seppelt, bringing together two Victorian wine businesses with a shared appreciation for great Australian wine, heritage and regional winemaking.

“Seppelt holds a distinctive place in Australian wine, with a proud history shaped by generations of winemakers, viticulturists and people across the business and its local communities,” Lilley said.

“For the people who know and love Seppelt, it’s a positive move that keeps the brand in Victorian hands. Its wines, heritage and place in the history of Australian wine are at the heart of what makes Seppelt special, and Aaron and his team are well placed to carry that forward.”

Buyer Aaron Drummond said Seppelt has produced some of the greatest wines in the country.

“It possesses such important vineyards and an incredible history. To be able to build on that tradition and reputation as a pioneer and leader for Australian sparkling and fine wine, is an absolute privilege.”

The sale is expected to be completed in mid-October 2026.

TWE said it is consulting directly with impacted team members at Seppelt sites and will support them closely through this change.

Seppelt’s roots date to 1851 when Joseph Seppelt established Seppeltsfield in the Barossa Valley. The Great Western winery was founded in 1865 and became part of Seppelt in 1918.

TWE said the site is renowned for its historic underground cellars, known as ‘The Drives’, which are the largest underground cellars in Australia and were first excavated by local gold miners in 1868. It added that the Drumborg vineyard, first planted in 1964, also “reflects Seppelt’s pioneering approach to cool-climate viticulture and has become known for wines that express the distinctive conditions of south-western Victoria”.

The brand is recognised for its significant contribution to the development of Australian sparkling wine.

content:
Ben Pridham of Pridham Viticulture in McLaren Vale, SA, offers a follow-up to his self-published piece ‘The escalator we built and won’t use’, offered in the same spirit: not criticism, but an invitation to think differently about what comes next.

The response to the first piece told me something worth acting on: this industry wants to have this conversation. So here are a few questions worth putting on the table (not answers, starting points) for where this conversation could go next.

Over more than forty years around this industry, it’s hard not to notice the genuine flourishing of organisations built to serve it. Federal, national, state and regional bodies, alongside research and compliance organisations, each established with good intent and staffed by people who give an enormous amount of their time and expertise. Worth being clear at the outset: none of this is a criticism of those people, it’s a question about the structure they’re working within.

That structure was largely built in better times, most of it is funded through a mix of industry levies, subscriptions and government funding, and all three of those funding lines are under real pressure. Levy and subscription income shrinks as growers and wineries exit the industry, with no one filling the space behind them. Government funding is doing more of the heavy lifting than it used to, not because industry chose that path, but because oversupply and shrinking sales have made it necessary. Lee McLean’s own advocacy for federal structural adjustment support earlier this year was a direct response to exactly that gap. Is it sustainable to keep asking a shrinking base to fully fund a structure that was sized for a larger one? That seems like a fair question to at least ask out loud.

So, the question isn’t whether our organisations are working hard — clearly, they are — it’s whether the shape of the sector: the number of separate bodies, each with its own board, its own leadership, its own overheads, often working on adjacent or overlapping ground, is still fit for purpose. Silos aren’t just an inefficiency, they’re where duplicated effort tends to hide, and duplicated effort is exactly what a shrinking funding base can least afford.

There’s a link here to the succession question raised last time, worth spelling out rather than assuming. This industry currently funds a great many separate peak roles such as CEOs, managing directors and executive chairs, spread across federal, national, state, regional, research and compliance bodies. Every one of those chairs needs its own ready successor. Spread the same pool of experienced people across that many roles, and is it any wonder each vacancy feels like starting from scratch? Concentrate that same talent into a smaller number of properly resourced positions, and the “who’s ready to step up?” question gets a great deal easier to answer. That’s not a smaller ambition for the industry — it may be the more achievable one.

There’s a further constraint sitting underneath much of this, too, and it deserves its own airing. Many industry organisations operate under constitutions or articles of association that were drawn up for a narrower purpose than the one the industry now needs solved. Those founding documents often exist for good reason: they keep an organisation focused on what it does well, but they can also quietly rule out avenues an organisation might otherwise be free to explore. In a climate where grapegrowers and wine companies badly need every legitimate channel of diversification kept open to them, is it worth asking whether some organisations’ own constitutions have become one of the things standing in the way? Not through anyone’s design, but simply because they were never written with today’s economics in mind? If part of the answer to underpinning producers going forward is more diversified economics, do our own governing documents need to diversify a little as well?

None of this is hypothetical, either. Australian Grape & Wine (the same organisation whose CEO search opened the first piece in this series) exists today only because two separate national bodies, the Winemakers’ Federation of Australia and Australian Vignerons, took exactly this kind of look at themselves in 2018 and voted to amalgamate into one. That happened because industry itself pushed for it, not because anyone was forced into it. If that was possible at national level once, is it really so far-fetched to ask the same question again at state and regional level, or between research and compliance functions?

There’s a useful external comparison, too. In 2002, the Wine Institute of New Zealand and the New Zealand Grape Growers Council merged into a single body, New Zealand Winegrowers, after identifying (in almost identical language to what’s on the table here) “significant overlaps in mandate and operations.” More than two decades on, New Zealand remains, by its own account, the only wine-producing country in the world with a single national industry body covering both growers and winemakers. Australia manages broadly similar functions across a considerably larger number of organisations. That’s not a criticism of anyone currently doing the work, it’s a genuine question about whether our scale still matches our structure.

None of what follows is a finished plan, it’s genuinely scratching the surface, and better to be wrong about the specifics and right about the need for the conversation than the reverse. A few starting ideas offered as prompts, not conclusions:

  • Task-sharing rather than duplication

Could a national body commission or “farm out” specific projects to the state or regional organisations best placed to deliver them, rather than every body building the same capability in parallel? Regional organisations often have the on-ground relationships whilst national bodies often have the scale and the government access. Right now, the tendency is to build both, everywhere, rather than pairing the two.

  • A genuine fit-for-purpose review, not just a funding review

Governance guidance for not-for-profits already expects boards to keep succession on the agenda and maintain a visible leadership pipeline. Could that same discipline extend to structure? Not just “can we afford this body next year?”, but “does this body’s function still need to sit where it currently sits, on its own, with its own executive team?”.

  • Revisiting the fine print, not just the org chart

Could organisations review their own constitutions and articles of association specifically through a diversification lens? Not to abandon their core purpose, but to test whether boundaries drawn decades ago still make sense for producers who now need support through more diversified economics, not just the traditional levers?

  • Shared services where the function is truly common

Compliance, research administration, secretariat functions — some of this is genuinely specialised to a state or region, and some of it isn’t. Where it isn’t, is sharing it really a loss of independence, or is it freeing up funding and people for the work that actually is specific to that patch?

  • A harder look at what “independence” is actually protecting

Every organisation has good reasons, in isolation, to remain its own entity; those reasons aren’t being dismissed here. The question is whether, added up across a dozen bodies, they still serve growers and winemakers as well as a smaller number of well-resourced, well-led organisations might.

This is a significant mindset shift to even raise, and it isn’t raised lightly. This industry is not short of capable people — the first piece argued exactly that, and nothing here changes that view — what might be worth testing is whether the way the sector has organised itself still matches the industry it actually has today, rather than the one this structure was originally built for. The future of this industry may lie less in what we already do and more in what we’re willing to imagine doing differently, and then actually do.

This is deliberately an open door, not a closed argument. Genuinely keen to hear where growers, winemakers and the people running these organisations agree, disagree, or would take any of this further. That disagreement is the point.

content:
TAFE NSW Sydney Wine Academy was ‘Highly Commended’ at the WSET’s Excellence in Education Awards. Image supplied

WSET has announced the winners of its inaugural Excellence in Education Awards, with TAFE NSW Sydney Wine Academy being ‘Highly Commended’ in the ‘Student Experience Award’ category.

The award was given for the course provider’s “role in developing the next generation of wine professionals through high-quality education and industry engagement”.

“This recognition is a testament to the passion, expertise and dedication of our educators and industry partners who are committed to developing the next generation of wine professionals,” said the TAFE NSW Sydney Wine Academy.

The awards, presented in a virtual ceremony at WSET’s annual Global APP Summit, recognise excellence across three categories: ‘Enterprise’, ‘Student Experience’ and ‘Social Impact’. The winners and highly commended recipients span six countries across three continents. The awards attracted 110 submissions from across 28 countries and territories.

“Course providers are at the heart of everything we do at WSET. They bring our qualifications to life, inspire learners and help us fulfil our purpose of empowering people and supporting the drinks industry from producer to consumer,” said Michelle Brampton, CEO of WSET.

“We launched the Excellence in Education Awards to recognise and celebrate that contribution. The quality of submissions was exceptional, and I’m delighted to see the achievements of our winners and highly commended recipients recognised today.”

Award winners included Academie du Vin Co Ltd. in Japan, recipient of the Enterprise Award for its “innovative WSET Sake Week campaign that generated record enrolments and engaged new audiences in sake education”; WiSP in France, winner of the Student Experience Award “for its personalised and inclusive approach to learning, combining expert teaching with innovative educational tools”; and The International Wine Education Centre (South Africa) received the Social Impact Award “for its long-standing commitment to widening access to drinks education and creating opportunities for learners from previously disadvantaged backgrounds”.

content:
New Zealand Winegrowers (NZW) has released its 2026 Annual Report, with exports reaching $2.108 billion and export volume increasing to 306.2 million litres in the 12 months to June 2026.

NZW said the result “reflects an overall sales increase of 8% driven by export growth and represents the industry’s second-highest June year total on record”.

“In the face of a challenging global and domestic environment, New Zealand wine continued to outperform the wider category in key markets, providing grounds for confidence in the long-term prospects of New Zealand wine,” it said.

Meanwhile, individual businesses across the sector were making adjustments. Vintage 2026 delivered a smaller harvest of approximately 440,000 tonnes, down a significant 15% on the previous year, bringing production “into closer balance with current market demand and supporting the industry’s focus on sustainable long-term growth”.

Fabian Yukich, chair of New Zealand Winegrowers, said the report showed an industry that was far from standing still.

“This has been a challenging year across the global wine industry, but New Zealand wine continues to show remarkable resilience.

“What stands out is the determination of growers and wineries to adapt. Businesses in the sector are making adjustments, the progress made this year gives us confidence that it is moving towards a more balanced footing”.

Yukich added that the report demonstrated the sector’s resilience.

“Consumers around the world continue to discover, love and buy New Zealand wines. Our focus is on supporting members through the immediate challenges while continuing to strengthen the opportunities that will carry the industry forward.”

CEO Anishka Jelicich, who was appointed to the role in July, said the Annual Report marked the start of the next phase for NZW, guided by its new strategy.

“Our new strategy has a clear purpose: to elevate and sustain the New Zealand wine industry by empowering our members,” Jelicich said.

“This means giving growers and wineries the information, advocacy and practical support they need to make well-informed decisions.”

Jelicich said NZW’s focus would be on turning the strategy into value for members.

“Our role is to support the industry as a whole so that New Zealand wine can emerge stronger and succeed over the long term”.

content:
Robyn Puglisi-Henderson is now the fourth member of the Puglisi family to receive the award. Images supplied

Robyn Puglisi-Henderson, business manager at Ballandean Estate Wines, has been honoured with the 2026 Samuel Bassett Award at the 42nd Annual Queensland Wine Awards.

The award is the Queensland wine industry’s highest mark of tribute, recognising long-term contribution and leadership.

Puglisi-Henderson is a fourth-generation member of the Puglisi family, the founders and custodians of Queensland’s oldest family-run winery, Ballandean Estate.

She has played a “vital role in the growth and resilience of the business for more than 25 years, since returning to the estate in 1999”.

“Among Robyn’s standout achievements is developing the estate’s export trade from zero to 20 per cent of business turnover in just five years, including establishing a market in China for the Granite Belt’s premium red wine,” said Adam Penberthy, president of the Queensland Wine Industry Association.

“The Samuel Bassett Award celebrates those who believe in what we do, who aren’t afraid to hold our ground in the face of the doubters, and who leave the industry better placed than they found it.”

Robyn with Adam Penberthy, president of the Queensland Wine Industry Association.

With this win, Robyn becomes the fourth member of the Puglisi family to receive the Samuel Bassett Award, following her father Angelo Puglisi (2003), her mother Mary Puglisi (2015) and her sister Leeanne Puglisi-Gangemi (2019).

“We opened the cellar the year I was born. I think I’ve spent more time there talking to people than I have at home! Being part of the Granite Belt’s tourism story for over 50 years is an honour. This week, we saw Stanthorpe awarded Gold at the 2026 Australian Top Tourism Town Awards. What a journey,” exclaimed Robyn Puglisi-Henderson.

“I was raised in a proud winemaking family. and it is my job and my hobby to champion Queensland wine. It is a pleasure to be part of such a great community who share the same passion for premium wine and visitor experiences.”

The winery shared that her work reflects the “essential, often less visible efforts that sustain a regional wine industry: building resilient businesses, creating new markets, supporting people and ensuring that the achievements of one generation become the foundations for the next”. Her contribution to the wider community was also recognised in 2016, when she received a Paul Harris Fellow Award for Community Service.

The Samuel Bassett Award is named for wine industry pioneer Samuel Symons Bassett, who hauled the first wine grape cuttings to Roma in 1863, laying an early foundation for winemaking in Queensland.

title: APISWA appoints Ian McKendrick as executive director
summary:
The Asia Pacific International Spirits and Wines Alliance (APISWA) has appointed Ian McKendrick as its new executive director. McKendrick will lead the Alliance’s engagement with governments, regulators and industry stakeholders across Asia Pacific, working with its 10 member companies to “strengthen the sector’s voice, promote evidence-based policy and support responsible growth”. “I am delighted to be joining APISWA. Asia Pacific is one of the most dynamic and significant regions for the international spirits and wine industry, and the policy environment is evolving rapidly across its markets. I look forward to working with our members, governments and partners to help shape that environment, from trade and taxation to responsible consumption and the fight against illicit alcohol, in ways that benefit consumers, local communities, and the wider economies in which our members operate,” McKendrick said.

content:
Ian McKendrick, the newly appointed executive director of APISWA. Image supplied

The Asia Pacific International Spirits and Wines Alliance (APISWA) has appointed Ian McKendrick as its new executive director.

McKendrick will lead the Alliance’s engagement with governments, regulators and industry stakeholders across Asia Pacific, working with its 10 member companies to “strengthen the sector’s voice, promote evidence-based policy and support responsible growth”.

“I am delighted to be joining APISWA. Asia Pacific is one of the most dynamic and significant regions for the international spirits and wine industry, and the policy environment is evolving rapidly across its markets.

“I look forward to working with our members, governments and partners to help shape that environment, from trade and taxation to responsible consumption and the fight against illicit alcohol, in ways that benefit consumers, local communities, and the wider economies in which our members operate,” McKendrick said.

Ludovic Ledru, chairman of APISWA, said the organisation is pleased to welcome McKendrick.

“His experience at the Scotch Whisky Association and in international trade diplomacy, including in China, makes him well suited to lead the Alliance at a time when the regulatory and policy landscape across Asia Pacific is becoming increasingly complex.

“Ian’s understanding of how governments, industry, and stakeholders can work together will be a real asset as we continue to champion the interests of our members and the responsible enjoyment of spirits and wine across the region,” Ledru said.

He joins APISWA from the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO). Prior to that, he spent six years at the Scotch Whisky Association (SWA), where he was international director, leading the association’s work to support the global growth of Scotch Whisky across more than 160 markets. He also spent more than two decades in the FCO, including postings at the British Embassy in Beijing and four years in the Directorate-General for Trade at the European Commission as a seconded national expert on China. His broader diplomatic career spanned economic and trade issues, including as lead negotiator for post-Brexit international agreements in the Middle East and North Africa.

content:
Kilikanoon Wines have had great success at the Mundus Vini awards in the past, being named ‘Best Australian Producer’ nine times. Image supplied

Clare Valley winery Kilikanoon Wines has taken home the title of ‘Best Producer Australia’ as well as the award for ‘Best Australian Red of Show’ with its Attunga 1865 Shiraz 2022 at the 2026 Mundus Vini Grand International Wine Awards.

The Mundus Vini awards are judged internationally, with wines assessed alongside entries from leading producers around the world.

Kilikanoon said the result is particularly meaningful given its long history of success at Mundus Vini, having previously been named ‘Best Australian Producer’ a record nine times.

Kilikanoon CEO Travis Fuller said the result was a great reflection of the team and the wines being made at the winery.

“To be named ‘Best Australian Producer’ and then have Attunga 1865 named ‘Best Australian Red of Show’, is a pretty special result for the team.

“There are some incredible Australian producers putting wines into these competitions, so to come out on top is something we’re really proud of.

“And to have that recognition come alongside another ‘Top 5 Red Star’ result from Halliday is a great reflection of the consistency of the wines we’re making.”

At the centre of the Mundus Vini result is the Attunga 1865 Shiraz, made from fruit grown on Kilikanoon’s historic Attunga vineyard. Planted in 1865, the vineyard is one of the Clare Valley’s oldest continuously producing Shiraz vineyards and has long been an important part of Kilikanoon’s premium red wine collection.

“It’s a great result for Clare Valley as well,” said Fuller.

“We know how good the wines being made here are, so it’s pretty special to see one of our wines recognised at this level.”

Kilikanoon Wines was established in 1997 and is based at a restored 1860s farmhouse in Penwortham, Clare Valley.

title: Coonawarra in for three weekends of Cabernet Celebrations
summary:
The Coonawarra Cabernet Celebrations are set to return this year from 1-18 October across three weekends of wine, food, music and regional experiences. Celebrating Coonawarra’s signature variety, Cabernet Sauvignon, this year’s festival features more than 40 free and ticketed experiences across the region, “inviting visitors to meet the makers, explore the vineyards and cellar doors and discover just why Coonawarra Cabernet has earned an international reputation”. Coonawarra is set to come alive this October with three weekends of Cabernet Celebrations. Image supplied

The Coonawarra Cabernet Celebrations are set to return this year from 1-18 October across three weekends of wine, food, music and regional experiences.

Celebrating Coonawarra’s signature variety, Cabernet Sauvignon, this year’s festival features more than 40 free and ticketed experiences across the region, “inviting visitors to meet the makers, explore the vineyards and cellar doors and discover just why Coonawarra Cabernet has earned an international reputation”.

Coonawarra Vignerons acting executive officer Heidi Guyett said the program of events provides a perfect reason to visit the region in spring.

“October is a fantastic time to experience Coonawarra. The vineyards are bursting back to life, the days are getting longer and there’s a wonderful energy throughout the region.

“Aside from tasting the exquisite wines of the region, visitors will have the opportunity to meet and dine with winemakers, viticulturists and boutique winery owners, go behind the scenes in the winery and even sample wines that are yet to be officially released, all the while learning about the process and the passion that goes into Coonawarra’s famed wines,” Guyett shared.

‘Something different every weekend’

The celebrations will begin over the October SA Labour Day long weekend, with the popular ‘Coonawarra Cabernet Celebrations Golf Day’ teeing off at Penola Golf Course on Friday 2 October.

The all-inclusive Ambrose event combines golf with sparkling Cabernet, regional food and Coonawarra wine, with teams competing for the “coveted Champion Team red jackets”.

Across the long weekend, visitors can also roll up their sleeves for ‘Pasta Making & Lunch with the DiGiorgio Family’, take a guided vineyard tour at Rymill Coonawarra, enjoy sparkling Cabernet at Sunset at Balnaves, or settle in for live music, pizza and family-friendly festivities at wineries across the region.

New to the festival in 2026, the ‘Coonawarra Community Markets’ will make their Cabernet Celebrations debut on Sunday 4 October, “showcasing the best of local with fresh produce, handmade and handcrafted goods, artisan wares and Coonawarra wines, all coming together in a vibrant community market atmosphere”.

The weekend of the 9 -11 October invites visitors to ‘Blend It Up’, with Cabernet Gin in the spotlight at Parker Estate, ‘Cocktails on the Deck’ on offer at Brand’s Laira and a relaxed afternoon of pizza and live music at Zema Estate.

The festival culminates with a feature-packed final weekend, led by the ‘Cabernet Decade[nce] Tasting and Dinner’ on Friday 16 October. Up to 15 Coonawarra producers will come together at Wynns Coonawarra Estate for a one-night-only tasting showcasing Cabernet Sauvignon with age, followed by an optional degustation dinner at the Ottelia Restaurant.

Saturday 17 October with feature Yalumba’s barrel Cooper demonstration at the Menzies Coonawarra property, set to be a highlight among the traditional offerings, including Bowen Estate’s ‘En Primeur’, a special ‘Decade of Majella Cabernet’ vertical tasting and ‘Prof’s Paella’ at Majella.

Another new addition to the program is the highly anticipated ‘Band on the Bus – Tipples and Tunes Road Tour’, combining great wine and live music in one roving day out. Guests will hop aboard for a tour of three wineries with Lady & The Amp jumping off the bus to perform a live set at each stop along the way.

Haylie Gregor from Lady & The Amp said the pair were looking forward to taking their music on the road.

“We’re really excited to bring the Band on the Bus concept into the Cabernet Celebrations program for the first time. It’s going to be a great day of Coonawarra wine, live music and plenty of laughs, and we can’t wait to have everyone on board.”

The program also features unique dining experiences such as ‘Brand’s Laira’s Dinner’ in Erics historic Cellar and Raidis Estate’s ‘Murder in the Vines – Mystery Dinner’ where guests are invited to “step back in time for an immersive evening of costumes, mystery and Coonawarra history, inspired by colourful characters from the region’s past”.

“Last year’s ‘Murder in the Vines’ was an absolute hit, so we knew we had to bring it back for another instalment,” said Raidis Estate co-owner Emma Raidis.

“It’s everything we love at Raidis — great wine, good food, plenty of laughs and people coming together.

“Guests are encouraged to embrace the 1920s theme, dress the part and immerse themselves in the story. If last year is anything to go by, there’ll be plenty of accusations, surprises and laughs along the way.”

‘Cabernet beyond the current vintage’

For those wanting to delve deeper, Cabernet Celebrations “provides a rare opportunity to discover Coonawarra wines across vintages, producers and styles”.

Museum wines, vertical tastings, pre-release wines and specially curated flights will feature throughout October, alongside experiences exploring food and wine pairings, vineyard stories and the “remarkable ageing potential” of Coonawarra Cabernet Sauvignon.

“One of the great things about the festival is the access it gives visitors to wines and experiences they might not ordinarily encounter,” Guyett said.

“There are opportunities to taste Cabernet across decades, try wines before release, walk through the vineyards and hear directly from the people who grow and make them. But equally, you can come along for pizza, music and a glass of wine on the lawn. There really is something for every kind of visitor.”

‘Leave the car behind’

For those venturing to the region, Coonawarra Vignerons emphasised that navigating the region “is a breeze with the region’s cellar doors all scattered along one stretch of road”.

Making it easier to explore the region, the ‘Coonawarra Cabernet Celebrations Hop On-Hop Off Shuttle Bus’ will operate exclusively on Saturdays 3, 10 and 17 October.

Nearby Blue Lake City residents can also ditch their keys with a newly introduced service from Mount Gambier departing at 10am, “making a day trip to Coonawarra easier than ever”.

Local hop-on hop-off tickets from Penola/Coonawarra are $23.50 per person, while the Mount Gambier return service, including all-day hop-on hop-off access, is $40 per person.

The shuttle is about making it easy for people to enjoy a full day in Coonawarra,” Guyett said.

“Whether you’re staying locally or visiting from Mount Gambier, you can leave the car behind, hop between participating wineries and events, and simply enjoy the day.”

Visitors are encouraged to book early, particularly for ticketed events, accommodation and Saturday shuttle services.

Treasury Wine Estates (TWE) has announced it will sell Seppelt to Aaron Drummond, CEO and co-owner of respected Mornington Peninsula winery Stonier, and partners.

The sale includes the Seppelt brand, the Great Western winery, cellar door and vineyards, and the Drumborg vineyard near Portland.

At its June Investor Day, TWE announced plans to explore the sale of “non-core brands and assets” as part of its “broader transformation to create a more focused brand portfolio and simplified production footprint”.

Treasury Wine Estates managing director, Australia & New Zealand and Europe, Angus Lilley said the sale was a positive outcome for Seppelt, bringing together two Victorian wine businesses with a shared appreciation for great Australian wine, heritage and regional winemaking.

“Seppelt holds a distinctive place in Australian wine, with a proud history shaped by generations of winemakers, viticulturists and people across the business and its local communities,” Lilley said.

“For the people who know and love Seppelt, it’s a positive move that keeps the brand in Victorian hands. Its wines, heritage and place in the history of Australian wine are at the heart of what makes Seppelt special, and Aaron and his team are well placed to carry that forward.”

Buyer Aaron Drummond said Seppelt has produced some of the greatest wines in the country.

“It possesses such important vineyards and an incredible history. To be able to build on that tradition and reputation as a pioneer and leader for Australian sparkling and fine wine, is an absolute privilege.”

The sale is expected to be completed in mid-October 2026.

TWE said it is consulting directly with impacted team members at Seppelt sites and will support them closely through this change.

Seppelt’s roots date to 1851 when Joseph Seppelt established Seppeltsfield in the Barossa Valley. The Great Western winery was founded in 1865 and became part of Seppelt in 1918.

TWE said the site is renowned for its historic underground cellars, known as ‘The Drives’, which are the largest underground cellars in Australia and were first excavated by local gold miners in 1868. It added that the Drumborg vineyard, first planted in 1964, also “reflects Seppelt’s pioneering approach to cool-climate viticulture and has become known for wines that express the distinctive conditions of south-western Victoria”.

The brand is recognised for its significant contribution to the development of Australian sparkling wine.

content:
Ben Pridham of Pridham Viticulture in McLaren Vale, SA, offers a follow-up to his self-published piece ‘The escalator we built and won’t use’, offered in the same spirit: not criticism, but an invitation to think differently about what comes next.

The response to the first piece told me something worth acting on: this industry wants to have this conversation. So here are a few questions worth putting on the table (not answers, starting points) for where this conversation could go next.

Over more than forty years around this industry, it’s hard not to notice the genuine flourishing of organisations built to serve it. Federal, national, state and regional bodies, alongside research and compliance organisations, each established with good intent and staffed by people who give an enormous amount of their time and expertise. Worth being clear at the outset: none of this is a criticism of those people, it’s a question about the structure they’re working within.

That structure was largely built in better times, most of it is funded through a mix of industry levies, subscriptions and government funding, and all three of those funding lines are under real pressure. Levy and subscription income shrinks as growers and wineries exit the industry, with no one filling the space behind them. Government funding is doing more of the heavy lifting than it used to, not because industry chose that path, but because oversupply and shrinking sales have made it necessary. Lee McLean’s own advocacy for federal structural adjustment support earlier this year was a direct response to exactly that gap. Is it sustainable to keep asking a shrinking base to fully fund a structure that was sized for a larger one? That seems like a fair question to at least ask out loud.

So, the question isn’t whether our organisations are working hard — clearly, they are — it’s whether the shape of the sector: the number of separate bodies, each with its own board, its own leadership, its own overheads, often working on adjacent or overlapping ground, is still fit for purpose. Silos aren’t just an inefficiency, they’re where duplicated effort tends to hide, and duplicated effort is exactly what a shrinking funding base can least afford.

There’s a link here to the succession question raised last time, worth spelling out rather than assuming. This industry currently funds a great many separate peak roles such as CEOs, managing directors and executive chairs, spread across federal, national, state, regional, research and compliance bodies. Every one of those chairs needs its own ready successor. Spread the same pool of experienced people across that many roles, and is it any wonder each vacancy feels like starting from scratch? Concentrate that same talent into a smaller number of properly resourced positions, and the “who’s ready to step up?” question gets a great deal easier to answer. That’s not a smaller ambition for the industry — it may be the more achievable one.

There’s a further constraint sitting underneath much of this, too, and it deserves its own airing. Many industry organisations operate under constitutions or articles of association that were drawn up for a narrower purpose than the one the industry now needs solved. Those founding documents often exist for good reason: they keep an organisation focused on what it does well, but they can also quietly rule out avenues an organisation might otherwise be free to explore. In a climate where grapegrowers and wine companies badly need every legitimate channel of diversification kept open to them, is it worth asking whether some organisations’ own constitutions have become one of the things standing in the way? Not through anyone’s design, but simply because they were never written with today’s economics in mind? If part of the answer to underpinning producers going forward is more diversified economics, do our own governing documents need to diversify a little as well?

None of this is hypothetical, either. Australian Grape & Wine (the same organisation whose CEO search opened the first piece in this series) exists today only because two separate national bodies, the Winemakers’ Federation of Australia and Australian Vignerons, took exactly this kind of look at themselves in 2018 and voted to amalgamate into one. That happened because industry itself pushed for it, not because anyone was forced into it. If that was possible at national level once, is it really so far-fetched to ask the same question again at state and regional level, or between research and compliance functions?

There’s a useful external comparison, too. In 2002, the Wine Institute of New Zealand and the New Zealand Grape Growers Council merged into a single body, New Zealand Winegrowers, after identifying (in almost identical language to what’s on the table here) “significant overlaps in mandate and operations.” More than two decades on, New Zealand remains, by its own account, the only wine-producing country in the world with a single national industry body covering both growers and winemakers. Australia manages broadly similar functions across a considerably larger number of organisations. That’s not a criticism of anyone currently doing the work, it’s a genuine question about whether our scale still matches our structure.

None of what follows is a finished plan, it’s genuinely scratching the surface, and better to be wrong about the specifics and right about the need for the conversation than the reverse. A few starting ideas offered as prompts, not conclusions:

  • Task-sharing rather than duplication

Could a national body commission or “farm out” specific projects to the state or regional organisations best placed to deliver them, rather than every body building the same capability in parallel? Regional organisations often have the on-ground relationships whilst national bodies often have the scale and the government access. Right now, the tendency is to build both, everywhere, rather than pairing the two.

  • A genuine fit-for-purpose review, not just a funding review

Governance guidance for not-for-profits already expects boards to keep succession on the agenda and maintain a visible leadership pipeline. Could that same discipline extend to structure? Not just “can we afford this body next year?”, but “does this body’s function still need to sit where it currently sits, on its own, with its own executive team?”.

  • Revisiting the fine print, not just the org chart

Could organisations review their own constitutions and articles of association specifically through a diversification lens? Not to abandon their core purpose, but to test whether boundaries drawn decades ago still make sense for producers who now need support through more diversified economics, not just the traditional levers?

  • Shared services where the function is truly common

Compliance, research administration, secretariat functions — some of this is genuinely specialised to a state or region, and some of it isn’t. Where it isn’t, is sharing it really a loss of independence, or is it freeing up funding and people for the work that actually is specific to that patch?

  • A harder look at what “independence” is actually protecting

Every organisation has good reasons, in isolation, to remain its own entity; those reasons aren’t being dismissed here. The question is whether, added up across a dozen bodies, they still serve growers and winemakers as well as a smaller number of well-resourced, well-led organisations might.

This is a significant mindset shift to even raise, and it isn’t raised lightly. This industry is not short of capable people — the first piece argued exactly that, and nothing here changes that view — what might be worth testing is whether the way the sector has organised itself still matches the industry it actually has today, rather than the one this structure was originally built for. The future of this industry may lie less in what we already do and more in what we’re willing to imagine doing differently, and then actually do.

This is deliberately an open door, not a closed argument. Genuinely keen to hear where growers, winemakers and the people running these organisations agree, disagree, or would take any of this further. That disagreement is the point.

WSET has announced the winners of its inaugural Excellence in Education Awards, with TAFE NSW Sydney Wine Academy being ‘Highly Commended’ in the ‘Student Experience Award’ category.

The award was given for the course provider’s “role in developing the next generation of wine professionals through high-quality education and industry engagement”.

“This recognition is a testament to the passion, expertise and dedication of our educators and industry partners who are committed to developing the next generation of wine professionals,” said the TAFE NSW Sydney Wine Academy.

The awards, presented in a virtual ceremony at WSET’s annual Global APP Summit, recognise excellence across three categories: ‘Enterprise’, ‘Student Experience’ and ‘Social Impact’. The winners and highly commended recipients span six countries across three continents. The awards attracted 110 submissions from across 28 countries and territories.

“Course providers are at the heart of everything we do at WSET. They bring our qualifications to life, inspire learners and help us fulfil our purpose of empowering people and supporting the drinks industry from producer to consumer,” said Michelle Brampton, CEO of WSET.

“We launched the Excellence in Education Awards to recognise and celebrate that contribution. The quality of submissions was exceptional, and I’m delighted to see the achievements of our winners and highly commended recipients recognised today.”

Award winners included Academie du Vin Co Ltd. in Japan, recipient of the Enterprise Award for its “innovative WSET Sake Week campaign that generated record enrolments and engaged new audiences in sake education”; WiSP in France, winner of the Student Experience Award “for its personalised and inclusive approach to learning, combining expert teaching with innovative educational tools”; and The International Wine Education Centre (South Africa) received the Social Impact Award “for its long-standing commitment to widening access to drinks education and creating opportunities for learners from previously disadvantaged backgrounds”.
